TWO PROBLEMS IN COMPARATIVE PRIME NUMBER THEORY: THE
FIVE-WAY RACE MODULO 11, AND THE SIGN OF THE INTEGRATED
PRIME COUNTING ERROR
ZIYANG LIU† , YUNXUAN WANG† , AND YAO SHI*
Abstract. We resolve two problems of Hamieh, Kadiri, Martin and Ng in comparative prime
number theory. First, under the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) and the usual linearindependence hypothesis (LI), we compute all 120 logarithmic densities in the five-way prime
number race among the quadratic residues modulo 11. The densities form exactly eight symmetry classes. We give rigorous, pairwise disjoint enclosures for the eight values and hence prove
their strict order. The key reduction factors the limiting distribution into two radial laws; the
ordering then depends only on the ratio of their radii, replacing a four-dimensional integral
by a one-dimensional one. The same argument applies to contestants forming a coset of any
subgroup of (Z/qZ)∗ and counts the radial variables that remain.

1.2. The reduction behind Problem 20
Feuerverger and Martin [10] derived a general formula for race densities and evaluated it for
q ≤ 12 and at most four contestants. They identified the five-way race modulo 11 as a natural

integral whose integrand is a product over nine non-principal characters and thousands of zero
ordinates.

1.4. Proof architecture and organization
The proof of Theorem 1.1 has four stages:
character blocks =⇒ one radial ratio =⇒ angular intervals =⇒ certified densities.
Section 3 proves the first two arrows and the symmetry count. Section 4 controls the four
numerical inputs: zero lists, zero tails, angular measure, and radial measure. Section 5 assembles
the enclosures and proves that they are disjoint.
The proof of Theorem 1.2 follows a different four-stage chain:
integrated explicit formula =⇒ support criterion =⇒ q ≤ 60 =⇒ finite certification.
Sections 7–11 carry out these steps in order. Section 2 first records the certification machinery
shared by the two parts. In both parts Turing’s method proves that the computed zero lists
are complete, simple, and on the critical line; the omitted zeros are bounded analytically rather
than discarded.
2. The common method
The two halves of this paper answer different questions, and they run the same pipeline. This
section states it once. Each half then names only what is special to it.
2.1. Explicit formulae
Each half writes its error term as a sum over the nontrivial zeros of the Dirichlet L-functions
modulo q. The arithmetic enters through the ordinates of those zeros, and through nothing
else. The two halves use different kernels, and the difference decides how much work the tail
is. Problem 20 uses the kernel of the unintegrated error, where the amplitude of the zero ρ is
2/|ρ| and the series converges only in L2 . Problem 23 integrates once, which multiplies each
amplitude by 1/|ρ + 1| and makes the series converge absolutely.
2.2. Locating the zeros
We locate the zeros by a sign-change scan of the real-valued Hardy real-valued critical-line
function associated with each primitive character, on a fixed grid, followed by repeated bisection
of each sign change. Arb then certifies each bracket in ball arithmetic: the ball at each endpoint
excludes zero, and the two balls carry opposite signs. A certified bracket proves that a zero is
there. It does not prove that no zero was missed.
2.3. Completeness of the zero lists
Turing’s method proves completeness. Both halves use the same criterion, in the pair form of
Section 4.1, and both take its one external input from Theorem 2 of Rumely [27]. The criterion
proves three things at once: the scan missed no zero below the certified height, every zero it
counts is simple, and every zero it counts lies on the critical line. The direction of the logic is
safe. A zero missed inside the test window only makes the test quantity larger, so the criterion
can fail to certify, and it cannot certify falsely. The pair counting identity behind the criterion
carries no additive constant, and that needs L(1/2, χ) 6= 0; each half certifies that non-vanishing
before it writes a zero file.
2.4. Ball arithmetic and certification
We use the word certified in one sense only: a quantity is certified when the number reported
for it is an enclosure that is proved to contain it. Every step that reaches a certified number is
carried out in Arb ball arithmetic, at a working precision that the run raises until the required
separation holds.

Neither half discards them, and neither half estimates them from a smooth zero density. Each
bounds them in closed form. Problem 20 subtracts exact moments of the ordinates and bounds

3. A formula for the densities
This section recalls the limiting distribution of Rubinstein and Sarnak [26], records the formula
of Feuerverger and Martin [10] for the densities, and then writes that formula in coordinates
adapted to the five contestants of this paper. The result is Theorem 3.3: one integral in one

The one new step is the regrouping of its character product by the discrete Fourier transform

of the same argument, Theorem 3.6. It counts the radial variables of a race on a coset of any
subgroup of (Z/qZ)∗ , and the last subsection checks it at n = 4 against the published four-way
race modulo 5.

The six break points have a geometric description as a transversality discriminant. The

low zeros from an ordering distribution remains open and belongs to a separate inverse problem.
